EXTERNAL FRAMING — Fowler/Böckeler "Harness Engineering for Coding Agents" (martinfowler.com/articles/harness-engineering.html, reviewed 2026-06-01)

This epic is the project's primary BEHAVIOUR-HARNESS sensor in the article's taxonomy (Agent = Model + Harness; guides=feedforward, sensors=feedback). Three load-bearing implications:

1. STRATEGIC JUSTIFICATION for north-star/P0. The article names the behaviour harness (functional correctness) as the least-mature, hardest harness category, and pins the root cause precisely: current AI-coding pipelines 'put a lot of faith into AI-generated tests — that's not good enough yet.' DSO's correctness story rests on agent-authored RED tests + completion-verifier with NO computational ground-truth that a passing test would fail if behaviour broke. Mutation testing IS that missing computational sensor. The article independently arrives at this epic's thesis (its 'Context' section), and explicitly cites the 'resurgence of mutation and structural testing as computational feedback sensors' as current best practice. External corroboration that this is the right P0 bet.

2. COMPUTATIONAL vs INFERENTIAL — placement is validated. The article distinguishes cheap deterministic sensors from expensive probabilistic LLM ones, and says inferential sensors (our code-reviewer-test-quality change-detector check) are 'expensive and probabilistic.' Mutation testing is the COMPUTATIONAL backstop that gives that inferential sensor empirical ground truth. They are complementary, not redundant: test-quality-gate catches obvious change-detectors pre-commit (cheap, left); mutation testing proves catch-power post-integration (the article's 'keep quality left' cost/speed distribution — slow sensors belong in the post-integration pipeline, exactly where SC2/SC3 place this as a non-blocking CI job). No re-scoping needed; this records WHY the architecture matches external best practice.

3. SILENT-SENSOR CAUTION — sharpens SC4. The article flags an open problem directly relevant here: 'interpreting silent sensors — do they indicate quality or inadequate detection?' For mutation testing this is the high-kill-rate trap: a 95% kill rate can mean strong tests OR weak/few mutants. The epic already partially guards this (mutants_generated as a DISTINCT field; SC4 self-reflection prompt about non-test-PR windows). The article reinforces that mutant-generation ADEQUACY — not just kill rate — must be visible to the maintainer at threshold-setting time (SC4) and at enforcement (SC5). Consider surfacing low-mutant-count / narrow-operator-coverage as its own annotation so a 'silent' high score isn't misread as catch-power. No SC rewrite required; treat as a preplanning consideration for the SC4 reference table and SC5 enforcement gate.

4. STEERING LOOP — already designed in. The article's 'steering loop' (human iterates on the harness when sensors reveal recurring issues) is exactly this epic's indirect feedback path: surviving-mutant breach -> auto-bug -> /dso:fix-bug -> 69e8 negative-example graduation into test-writing prompts. Worth naming explicitly as the steering-loop instance it is.

No scope change proposed. Logged for preplanning context and to anchor the epic to external best-practice framing.
